html:
I took up basketball around 2002. It started when I broke my hand playing football and switched to basketball for good (sounds odd, but football just gets you injured too easily); the other reason was Yao Ming. My childhood friends all loved it too, so we played together a lot. I was obsessed back then: even in the ten-minute break between classes I’d grab the ball and run to the court, and back in class my head would be full of replays of the moves I’d just made. We only had Sunday afternoons off, and a few of us would go straight from school to the court, then to a restaurant to wolf down a feast. I loved every pass and every bit of teamwork with my buddies, loved showing off after a tough shot and seeing the amazed looks of the onlookers, loved everything that belonged to being young.

Later, at university, I had more free time but actually played less. Our class team was terrible, and lots of people played video games instead, so four years left me without many basketball memories. In my master’s I finally found strong teammates, and we won a few games across two league seasons.

After I went abroad, Sunday-afternoon basketball was a shot in the arm for me, newly arrived in a foreign land. I played myself into the ground every week and nodded off all through my boss’s lecture on Monday mornings. Then, once again thanks to football, I badly sprained my ankle. After a year and a half off I made a comeback, playing once or twice a week in the university gym and the odd pickup game outdoors.

In my year since moving from Germany to the Netherlands I barely played (my PhD thesis, darling!), until recently I found a local club. Now, as the only foreigner there, I hang out every Wednesday with players from the lowest league. After four sessions, yesterday I finally felt that long-lost basketball high again.

For anyone who loves basketball, that high is unrivaled, one of a kind. All these years basketball has been like an old friend: on and off, but always there. From running the full court endlessly with limitless energy in high school to now, at thirty, gradually becoming a below-the-rim player, time changes and space pulls us apart, but what stays the same is that pure love, and the heart that beats faster at the sound of a ball hitting the floor.
